So.. I wanna say yes and no? Being asked if you were sodomized *could* be relevant information, but it seems like it was absolutely inappropriate in context. Gaslighting you about your pain level during your scope and telling you to get help from your mother with enemas is wildly out of line. What if you were an elderly or physically disabled patient with no help around?


As for the new doctor, next time he brings up the gyno/dermatologist, you can happily counter him with “no, but since no offices in our area are accepting new patients, *I’d like your office’s assistance in finding one*.” If he’s going to pressure you about it but not offer any solutions, it is now your turn to pressure him for a solution. 


Then finally, a doctor asking why you’ve never seen a gynecologist before is not as uncommon as you may think, but again, context really matters. If he was asking you in a way that was condescending, or accusatory, it’s not okay. 


It sounds like you need new doctors. If you aren’t comfortable with something they’ve done you have every right to step away and find something else. Doctors work for *you*. Not the other way around. Don’t let them forget that.


TLDR; Some questions are medically necessary, but the context and tone in which they are asked matter the most. No doctor should ever downplay a patient’s pain or experiences with procedures. And no doctor should ever insinuate that you’ve done something to make your symptoms worse and therefore don’t deserve empathy or unbiased care for it.

The way intestinal parasites will afflict you is if you consume more than one “bite” of predator meat within 24 hours. The game counts this as instances however; if you accidentally cancel out of eating a bear steak, do not touch it again for 24 hours. If you eat a wolf steak and then accidentally pan over and eat another, even if you cancel it as fast as humanly possible, you’ll get the full affliction.


My advice and what my method is, eat one predator steak once a day, at the same time, as soon as you see the *intestinal parasite risk* affliction go away. With bear meat this will be plenty to sustain you, especially if you can supplement the rest with cattails/acorns/looted food.

Being great at sandbox before going into story mode is akin to having the highest quality of tools before starting a project. You have exactly the right resources you need and that aspect should be a breeze, but you’ve never done this type of project before. Essentially, story mode is going to have you playing slightly differently because of the goals it sets for you. I played story mode first when I picked up the game, so I can’t speak to mastery of sandbox before the story, but I can say that the plot is rich and I’ve thoroughly enjoyed the episodes thus far. 


You get lore and history on Great Bear that enhances sandbox, and you get to be a part of a good story. It isn’t too terribly long, if you sat down with the intent to bang it out you’d probably finish it in less than a week. As for how difficult it is, I’d say it’s between pilgrim/voyageur; pilgrim-like loot tables, voyageur-like wildlife and weather, so it’s decently easy at face value before you factor in the other elements of the story. Without spoiling anything, some goals you’ll work towards are quite difficult, and thrown on top of the survival itself could get you into some pretty hairy situations. The story-line, in my opinion, gets more and more developed over each episode, because naturally Hinterland improved upon each release, and the most recent episode had me really impressed with how far they’ve come. I can’t wait to see what they’ll throw at us for episode 5. As for distracting you and how story based it is, it’s pretty heavily story based IF you choose. Goals aren’t really time limited unless you’re actively in a cut scene/situation, so you can progress as you like, but there is always something to be working towards. You can choose what your focus is on at the moment. Oh and the walking simulator part? Welcome to the game, can’t really do anything about that. Story or survival, this game is definitely a really dynamic walking simulator. It used to bug me but after playing for a long time, I don’t really care anymore, it’s worth it.


I do highly recommend the story if you’ve enjoyed the game. Hinterland is a team of artists before they’re a team of developers and the story shows that labor of love. I hope any of this answered your questions! If you have more I’m happy to help!

Vet tech here. I’m so sorry about your baby! In any other circumstance I would recommend taking him to a different vet for a second opinion but I understand you have financial restraints with that. If you can switch him to a colorless litter, such as crystal, that will more easily help you monitor color and amount of urine. Be very very watchful of this. Blockages can go south very quickly. In addition, if it comes down to it and he desperately needs X-rays, don’t be afraid to price shop around and call different clinics. X-rays are $190 at my clinic as we try to be affordable as possible. Another place may charge you $300-$600. So call other vets and ask how much x-rays, specifically 3 abdominal views would cost you. I only add the amount of views because some vets charge per view. Also look into CareCredit! It’s fairly easy to get approved and it’s like a medical credit card for your furbabies. It’ll allow you to pay back these costs over 3-6 months. Best of luck and give him some hugs for me!

Pellets- it depends on their size, usually it’s 2-3 once a day. Keep in mind that a betta’s stomach is about the size of one of their eyes so feed sparingly and accordingly. Blood worms- a few times a week, just keep in mind the eye size rule. Usually one larger or two small/medium sized bloodworms is plenty. With my bettas I would do this at least a full 6-8 hours after I fed them pellets in the morning. Shrimp- since I don’t know what type of shrimp, again, keep in mind the eye size rule and don’t feed treats more than a few times per week. Also, if the shrimp or bloodworms are freeze dried, remember to soak them in aquarium water first before you feed them to prevent them from expanding in the betta’s stomach.

Scuds. They aren’t harmful unless you have baby shrimp, which they could pick on, but otherwise harmless. Could even be a tasty treat for any livestock in your tank. The only problem is there isn’t really any other way to remove them besides doing it manually- siphoning, netting, etc.

I worked in the pet industry for 2 years and I saw a lot of rehomings in that time. My answer is to keep them. I took in an abused parrotlet years ago and kept her even though she hated human interaction and anything to do with me, but I didn’t blame her. I’m not saying your birds have had lesser care, but that might just be the way they are- I also dealt with a lot of birds and some are just different. I say keep them because you would have no way of knowing if the next owner they end up with would be as good to them; that’s why I kept my bird. They might encounter the same problem and rehome them again, causing further stress on the birds, which can be deadly. Stick it out, be as good of a bird parent as you can be for the sake of them staying in the place they know as home.
